title: Study of Compounds: Hydrogen Chloride
tagline: Study the preparation, properties and tests of hydrogen chloride gas and hydrochloric acid.

overview.intro: Hydrogen chloride (HCl) is a colourless, pungent gas that dissolves readily in water to form hydrochloric acid, an important laboratory and industrial acid. This chapter covers laboratory preparation of hydrogen chloride, its physical and chemical properties, the fountain experiment demonstrating high solubility, and characteristic reactions and tests of hydrochloric acid. Emphasis is placed on correct conditions, observations and equations.

facts.label: Formula
facts.value: HCl (gas); hydrochloric acid in aqueous solution

facts.label: Key property
facts.value: Highly soluble in water; acidic in solution

facts.label: Tests
facts.value: Dense white fumes with NH3; white precipitate with AgNO3

learningOutcomes: Describe laboratory preparation and collection of dry hydrogen chloride gas.
Explain physical properties including high solubility in water.
Describe chemical properties of hydrochloric acid with metals, bases and carbonates.
Identify tests for hydrogen chloride/hydrochloric acid and chloride ions.
Write balanced equations for preparation and characteristic reactions.

blocks.text: Hydrogen chloride gas is prepared in the laboratory by heating sodium chloride with concentrated sulphuric acid. At temperatures below about 200°C, sodium hydrogen sulphate and hydrogen chloride are formed: NaCl + H2SO4(conc.) → NaHSO4 + HCl↑. The reaction is carried out in a flask with controlled heating, and the gas is dried before collection if dry HCl is required.

Dry hydrogen chloride is collected by upward displacement of air (downward delivery) because it is denser than air and highly soluble in water, so it cannot be collected over water. Concentrated sulphuric acid is commonly used as a drying agent; alkaline drying agents are unsuitable because they react with acidic HCl gas.

items: Use concentrated sulphuric acid as a non-volatile acid to displace HCl.
Collect by downward delivery due to high density and water solubility.
Dry with concentrated H2SO4, not with quicklime or alkalis.
Avoid excessive heating that may lead to further reactions or hazards.

learn.title: Physical Properties and the Fountain Experiment

blocks.text: Hydrogen chloride is a colourless gas with a sharp, choking odour. It is denser than air and extremely soluble in water. When dissolved in water, it ionises to form hydrochloric acid, producing H3O+ and Cl− ions, which account for its acidic properties in aqueous solution.

The fountain experiment demonstrates the high solubility of HCl in water. A flask filled with dry HCl is fitted with a jet tube and connected to water containing blue litmus. When a small amount of water enters the flask, HCl dissolves rapidly, creating low pressure so that water rushes in as a fountain and turns red, showing formation of an acidic solution.

items.text: Dry HCl gas does not turn dry blue litmus red, but moist HCl does.
items.note: Acidic behaviour requires ionisation in presence of water.

items.text: Fountain experiment: water jets into HCl-filled flask and litmus changes to red.
items.note: Demonstrates both high solubility and acidic nature in solution.

blocks.text: Hydrochloric acid behaves as a typical acid in aqueous solution. It reacts with active metals such as zinc and magnesium to liberate hydrogen gas and form metal chlorides. It reacts with bases and alkalis in neutralisation to form salt and water, and with metal carbonates or bicarbonates to release carbon dioxide.

Hydrochloric acid also reacts with metal oxides to form corresponding chlorides and water. These reactions are useful for preparing soluble chloride salts and for identifying acidic behaviour. Dilute acid is commonly used in such tests unless otherwise specified.

learn.title: Tests for Hydrogen Chloride and Chlorides

blocks.text: Hydrogen chloride gas produces dense white fumes of ammonium chloride when a glass rod dipped in concentrated ammonia solution is brought near it. This is a sensitive test for HCl gas. In aqueous solution, hydrochloric acid turns blue litmus red and shows typical acid reactions.

Chloride ions in solution can be detected by adding silver nitrate solution in the presence of dilute nitric acid, which gives a white precipitate of silver chloride that is soluble in excess ammonium hydroxide. This test distinguishes chlorides from some other halides and confirms presence of Cl− ions.

items.meaning: Collection of a gas by allowing it to displace air downwards, used for gases denser than air.
An experiment showing high solubility of a gas in water by rapid suction of water into a flask.
Formation of white AgCl precipitate with AgNO3 as a test for chloride ions.

blocks.text: Hydrochloric acid is used in laboratories for preparing chlorides, cleaning metal surfaces (pickling), and adjusting pH in various processes. Hydrogen chloride gas and concentrated hydrochloric acid are corrosive and irritant, so they must be handled with care, proper ventilation and appropriate protective measures.

When preparing or using HCl, avoid inhaling fumes and prevent contact with skin and eyes. Reactions that generate hydrogen gas should be performed away from flames. Correct laboratory technique ensures both accurate observations and safety.

items: Use fume control when generating or testing HCl gas.
Add reagents carefully and follow prescribed heating conditions.
Store acids in labelled containers and handle with appropriate care.
Neutralise spills according to laboratory safety guidance.

keyPoints: HCl gas is prepared by reacting NaCl with concentrated H2SO4 under controlled heating.
Dry HCl is collected by downward delivery and dried with concentrated sulphuric acid.
HCl is highly soluble in water and forms hydrochloric acid, shown by the fountain experiment.
Dry HCl does not show acidic behaviour with dry litmus; moisture is required for ionisation.
Hydrochloric acid reacts with metals, bases, carbonates and oxides to form chlorides.
HCl gas gives dense white fumes with ammonia due to formation of ammonium chloride.
Chloride ions give a white precipitate of AgCl with silver nitrate in dilute nitric acid.
Balanced equations should reflect correct reactants, products and conditions.
Collection method depends on density and solubility of the gas.
Safety precautions are essential when handling corrosive acids and gases.
examFocus: Describe preparation, drying and collection of dry HCl gas with reasons.
Explain the fountain experiment and what it demonstrates.
Write equations for reactions of hydrochloric acid with metals, carbonates and bases.
State tests for HCl gas and for chloride ions in solution.
Explain why dry HCl does not turn dry blue litmus red.
Choose correct drying agents and reject unsuitable ones.
Use accurate observations such as dense white fumes and white precipitate.

vocabulary.meaning: A colourless, pungent gas (HCl) that forms hydrochloric acid in water.
The aqueous solution of hydrogen chloride, containing H3O+ and Cl− ions.
Method of collecting a gas denser than air by displacing air downwards.
A substance used to remove moisture from a gas.
Demonstration of high solubility of a gas in water causing a fountain effect.
Formation of ions when a substance dissolves in water.
Dense white fumes formed when HCl reacts with ammonia.
A white precipitate (AgCl) formed in the test for chloride ions.
Capable of damaging or destroying materials or living tissue by chemical action.
Bubbling or fizzing due to gas evolution in a liquid.
An acid with low tendency to vaporise, used to displace more volatile acids.

questions.prompt: Dry hydrogen chloride gas is collected by:
questions.answer: downward delivery
questions.explanation: HCl is denser than air and highly soluble in water, so it is collected by downward delivery.
questions.commonMistake: Do not collect highly soluble gases over water.

questions.prompt: The drying agent commonly used for HCl gas is:
questions.answer: concentrated sulphuric acid
questions.explanation: Concentrated H2SO4 dries acidic HCl without reacting with it.
questions.commonMistake: Alkaline substances react with HCl and cannot be used as drying agents.

questions.prompt: Dense white fumes are produced when HCl gas comes in contact with:
questions.answer: ammonia
questions.explanation: Ammonia reacts with hydrogen chloride to form white fumes of ammonium chloride.
questions.commonMistake: This is a characteristic identification test for HCl gas.

questions.prompt: The fountain experiment demonstrates that HCl is:
questions.answer: highly soluble in water
questions.explanation: Rapid dissolution of HCl creates low pressure, causing water to rush into the flask as a fountain.
questions.commonMistake: The experiment also shows acidic nature when litmus turns red.

questions.prompt: Dry hydrogen chloride gas does not turn dry blue litmus red because:
options: it does not ionise without water
questions.answer: it does not ionise without water
questions.explanation: Acidic behaviour requires formation of H+ (H3O+) ions in aqueous medium.
questions.commonMistake: HCl is acidic in water; dryness prevents ionisation.

questions.prompt: Hydrochloric acid reacts with zinc to produce:
questions.answer: zinc chloride and hydrogen
questions.explanation: Active metals react with dilute acids to liberate hydrogen gas and form salts.
questions.commonMistake: Identify the correct salt formed from hydrochloric acid (a chloride).

questions.prompt: A white precipitate soluble in excess NH4OH is formed when AgNO3 is added to a solution containing:
questions.answer: chloride ions
questions.explanation: Silver chloride is a white precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonium hydroxide.
questions.commonMistake: The test is carried out in presence of dilute nitric acid.

questions.prompt: In the laboratory preparation of HCl, concentrated H2SO4 is preferred because it is:
options: non-volatile and strong enough to displace HCl
questions.answer: non-volatile and strong enough to displace HCl
questions.explanation: A non-volatile acid can displace a more volatile acid like HCl from its salt on heating.
questions.commonMistake: Volatile acids would mix with the gas produced.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen chloride gas has a sharp, ________ odour.
questions.answer: pungent
questions.explanation: HCl is recognised by its characteristic pungent, irritating smell.
questions.commonMistake: Never inhale gases directly to test odour in a laboratory.

questions.prompt: The white fumes formed when HCl reacts with ammonia are ________.
questions.answer: ammonium chloride
questions.explanation: HCl and NH3 combine to form solid ammonium chloride particles seen as fumes.
questions.commonMistake: Write the correct chemical name of the product.

questions.prompt: HCl gas cannot be collected over water because it is highly ________ in water.
questions.answer: soluble
questions.explanation: High solubility would cause the gas to dissolve instead of being collected.
questions.commonMistake: Collection method must account for both solubility and density.

questions.prompt: Write the equation for laboratory preparation of hydrogen chloride from sodium chloride.
questions.answer: NaCl + H2SO4(conc.) → NaHSO4 + HCl↑ (on gentle heating below 200°C).
questions.explanation: Concentrated sulphuric acid displaces hydrogen chloride from sodium chloride.
questions.commonMistake: Indicate concentrated acid and appropriate conditions.

questions.prompt: Why is HCl gas not dried using quicklime?
questions.answer: Quicklime is basic and reacts with acidic hydrogen chloride gas, so it cannot be used as a drying agent. Concentrated sulphuric acid is used instead because it removes moisture without reacting with HCl.
questions.explanation: Drying agents must not chemically react with the gas being dried.
questions.commonMistake: Choose a drying agent compatible with the nature of the gas.

questions.prompt: Explain the fountain experiment for hydrogen chloride.
questions.answer: A flask is filled with dry HCl gas and fitted with a jet tube dipping into blue litmus solution. When a drop of water is introduced into the flask, HCl dissolves rapidly, creating a partial vacuum. Atmospheric pressure then forces the litmus solution up as a fountain into the flask, and it turns red, showing that HCl is highly soluble and forms an acidic solution.
questions.explanation: The experiment demonstrates both solubility and acidic nature in water.
questions.commonMistake: Mention the pressure change that causes the fountain effect.

questions.prompt: State what is observed when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to (i) zinc granules and (ii) sodium carbonate.
questions.answer: (i) Effervescence occurs due to evolution of hydrogen gas, and zinc chloride solution is formed. (ii) Brisk effervescence occurs due to evolution of carbon dioxide gas, and sodium chloride and water are formed.
questions.explanation: Different reactants produce characteristic gases with acids.
questions.commonMistake: Name the gas evolved in each case.

questions.prompt: Describe the laboratory preparation of dry hydrogen chloride gas, including drying and collection with reasons.
questions.answer: Place sodium chloride in a flask and add concentrated sulphuric acid, then heat gently to produce HCl gas: NaCl + H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HCl↑. Pass the gas through concentrated sulphuric acid in a wash bottle to dry it, as H2SO4 absorbs moisture without reacting with acidic HCl. Collect the dry gas by downward delivery because HCl is denser than air and highly soluble in water, making collection over water unsuitable.
questions.explanation: Each step—generation, drying and collection—is chosen based on properties of HCl.
questions.commonMistake: Give reasons for the drying agent and collection method.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference in behaviour of dry HCl gas and hydrochloric acid towards litmus, with reason.
questions.answer: Dry HCl gas does not change the colour of dry blue litmus paper because it does not ionise in the absence of water and therefore does not produce hydrogen ions. Hydrochloric acid, which is an aqueous solution of HCl, ionises to produce H3O+ (or H+) ions and turns blue litmus red. This shows that acidic properties are exhibited in aqueous solution due to ionisation.
questions.explanation: Presence of water is essential for HCl to show acidic character.
questions.commonMistake: Do not conclude that HCl is not an acid; it is acidic when dissolved in water.

questions.prompt: How would you identify (i) hydrogen chloride gas and (ii) chloride ions in a solution? Describe observations and equations where relevant.
questions.answer: (i) Bring a glass rod dipped in concentrated ammonia solution near the gas; dense white fumes of ammonium chloride are formed: NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl. Moist HCl also turns blue litmus red. (ii) To test for chloride ions, add silver nitrate solution to the solution acidified with dilute nitric acid; a white precipitate of silver chloride forms: AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO3. The precipitate dissolves in excess ammonium hydroxide, confirming chloride ions.
questions.explanation: Distinct tests confirm HCl gas and chloride ions in solution.
questions.commonMistake: Acidify with dilute nitric acid before adding AgNO3 to avoid interfering precipitates.

questions.prompt: A gas jar of HCl is inverted over a gas jar of ammonia. Predict and explain the observation.
questions.answer: Dense white fumes of ammonium chloride form near the junction and spread within the jars. Hydrogen chloride and ammonia gases diffuse and react directly to produce solid ammonium chloride: NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl. The fumes appear where the gases meet and react.
questions.explanation: The reaction demonstrates that HCl is an acidic gas reacting with basic ammonia.
questions.commonMistake: The product is a solid formed as fine particles, seen as white fumes.

questions.prompt: A student attempts to collect dry HCl gas over water and to dry it using calcium oxide. Identify two mistakes and correct them.
questions.answer: Collecting HCl over water is incorrect because HCl is highly soluble in water and will dissolve instead of being collected; it should be collected by downward delivery. Drying with calcium oxide is incorrect because CaO is basic and reacts with acidic HCl; concentrated sulphuric acid should be used as the drying agent.
questions.explanation: Both collection and drying methods must be compatible with HCl’s properties.
questions.commonMistake: Consider solubility, density and chemical reactivity when choosing apparatus materials.

questions.prompt: Explain why hydrochloric acid conducts electricity but dry hydrogen chloride gas does not.
questions.answer: Dry hydrogen chloride consists of covalent molecules and does not contain free ions, so it does not conduct electricity. When dissolved in water, HCl ionises to form hydronium (or hydrogen) ions and chloride ions: HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl−. These mobile ions in hydrochloric acid carry electric charge, enabling conduction.
questions.explanation: Electrical conduction in solutions requires presence of mobile ions.
questions.commonMistake: Link conduction directly to ionisation in aqueous solution.

questions.prompt: You are given dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute sulphuric acid in unlabelled bottles. Suggest one chemical test to distinguish them using a barium salt, with observation.
questions.answer: Add barium chloride solution to each acid. With dilute sulphuric acid, a white precipitate of barium sulphate forms: BaCl2 + H2SO4 → BaSO4↓ + 2HCl, which is insoluble in dilute acids. With dilute hydrochloric acid, no such white precipitate is formed. This distinguishes sulphuric acid from hydrochloric acid.
questions.explanation: Formation of insoluble barium sulphate is characteristic of sulphate ions from sulphuric acid.
questions.commonMistake: Use a suitable barium salt solution and note that barium chloride is soluble.
